data.entry_subject: Building Offense Between Us

feature_section_1.caption: The best offence is no offense!

paragraphs.text: There are three things I’ve always wanted to be: a farmer, a writer and hilarious. I feel satisfied enough with my efforts on the first two… but being hilarious… requires other people to ‘get me’ and lately every time I start to think folks out there appreciate my (overly punny sort of odd) sense of humor, someone drops a comment on our YouTube channel that reminds me… I’m probably just coming off like a jackass.

A few months after starting our Arillian Farm YouTube channel, I stumbled into some success with my “Happy Flipping Wednesday” video series. That started with me flipping off each of our three dogs to try to piggyback on a trend where people were giving the middle finger to their dogs to get their random, cute weird reactions. As it turned out, our dogs’ responses to the finger pointed our YouTube channel in the right direction. Each of those first three Happy Flipping Wednesday shorts, landed immediately in my top 10 viewed and liked videos, so naturally, I expanded it to my goats, chickens, fish in my pond. Folks were loving it. I got over twenty thousand views when I flipped off our goats!

It felt like I was carving a quirky little niche out for our channel. But then, I flipped off a flock of pigeons –startling them into taking flight at the moment that one Adele song about sending her love to her ex's new lover was crescendoing. That day, my finger struck a nerve with one of my viewers.

To me, profanity-infused language and gestures are as much a social dialect as a 'southern accent' or a 'Boston accent.' We pick up the language our peers use, and in many circles – like among my boyfriend and his sons, or in certain urban areas – generous profanity is simply part of the lexicon. And to me, that's fine. My boyfriend’s sons and their mom, for example, flip each other off constantly – it’s just a funny way of saying “I love you, you goofball.”

Unfortunately, my disgruntled viewer commented that she was reporting me because of it, so I panicked and unlisted the short and that was basically the end of Happy Flipping Wednesdays …and my shorts stopped getting distributed for a while.

It was frustrating to see my channel gaining traction and then suddenly grind to a halt because one person felt it was her job to make sure I was punished. On social media at least, it seems like one person’s negativity can out-weigh hundreds of folks’ lighthearted enjoyment.

Several months after the end of Happy Flipping Wednesdays, I was mystified and thrilled to see a group of teenagers jumping off the roof of a neighboring house into a pool (I assume there was a pool, but their back wall was actually impeding my view so it looked like they were just jumping into a void and disappearing). It reminded me of this episode of the Twilight Zone where some kids jumped into a pool and came up in a pond in a fairy land or something. I thought I’d happened upon YouTube Gold, so I made a short of the scene and captioned it “They’re probably jumping into a swimming pool”, “but wouldn’t it be fun if they were actually jumping into a wormhole”, “and came up in some other part of the universe?” One viewer apparently took my commentary to mean that I disliked the kids and wished they’d disappear, so he posted a comment about me being a bitter Karen (fortunately he didn’t report me to YouTube though).

I didn’t love being called a Karen, and I’d have preferred an anonymous dislike or something on that level, but I could kind of see how someone might mistake the whimsy I had intended for bitterness, so I revised and reposted the short and responded to that commenter with my own lighthearted gibe: "I don't wish anyone any ill will Chad, I just literally love the idea of wormholes. lol." To me that seems like how it should work. Call each other out for stuff, adjust (or don’t) and move on.

Demanding that someone be punished because they offended you like the Happy Flipping Wednesday Lady seems self righteous and aggressive to me –especially when there are so many less severe ways to not see content from YouTubers you don’t appreciate.

Lately I get the vibe that almost no one is invested in understanding anyone else’s perspective. The whole “silence is violence” movement, feels like folks are just looking for reasons to sound the alarm on or justify hostility against strangers with political views different than their own. So many people applaud the “admirable and brave” souls out there hatefully fighting bigotry with bigotry, but it just feels like hypocrisy to me.

There’s a growing list of what you cannot say and what you must say to prove that you aren’t hateful and it feels like some folks are basically setting diction traps and waiting for hapless dolts like me to say the wrong thing so they can rain down upon me with their righteous indignation.

For someone like me, who often struggles to find the right words in social situations (and often stumbles into the exact wrong thing to say), it just feels like green-lighting bullying: Whenever I fail to say the right thing in a situation, everyone around me is now encouraged to belittle and punish me for ‘not getting it’.

It reminds me of my first week of college, feeling totally out of place and homesick. I remember commenting to one of the few people I was actually bonding with, a girl named Larkin, something like, "No one has made fun of me at all since we've been here. It makes me think no one likes me." Without missing a beat, she just said, "Don’t be a shithead Jillian, I like you." Her jab meant the world to me.

To me, the pursuit of joy and encouraging joy in others should be more important than trying to punish offensive offenders into oblivion. We should all be compassionate and understanding towards others as much as possible and we should try to say the right thing, but no one should be forced to carry anyone else’s emotional baggage for them.
Condemnation and ridicule may frighten or shame someone into compliance, but with compassion and conversation, everyone might be able to grow and find peace.

The justice system should punish those who are intent on causing harm and everyone else should work out offenses peacefully amongst themselves. There’s no reason why strangers should be overly concerned with the punishment of folks they’ve never met. Tolerance, compassion and taking responsibility for yourself seem like the best path to a free, peaceful society.

data.entry_subject: The Legend of Uncle Pete

paragraphs.text: If you knew my Uncle Pete, you knew a legend. He had all the usual legendary characteristics: tall, intellectually and athletically gifted, disarming and intimidating in equal measure and at the right times. But he also started his collection of fire trucks in the most legendary way a person could:

He was driving home from work one day and saw that the local fire station was selling some old fire trucks (because they had just received a donation to buy new ones or something), so he just bought a fire truck as… like… an impulse buy –because he could. He left his car to pick up later, drove the fire truck home and parked it on the street in front of the house.

Uncle Pete went on to buy and restore dozens more fire trucks over the years. He and my aunt bought a house on a 5 acre property near Denver with a barn big enough to house three or four modern fire trucks. He also had a garage added to their home that was big enough to house another fire truck or two with a giant master suite on top of it.

He collected all sorts of fire gear and memorabilia (fireman hats from different eras and fire boots and fire hydrants). He even had a couple of Dalmatians: Seagraves (who was named after a fire truck) and Dally Dalmatian.

When I visited the Van Huysens as a child, I remember what a lively, happy pack of three or four big dogs they had running up and down the grassy slope and the winding dirt driveway between their house and the fire engine barn.

Uncle Pete was an animal lover. After my aunt and uncle said goodbye to their last dog, a herd of deer started taking refuge on their property and (when it wasn't rutting season) Uncle Pete would feed the deer (in spite of knowing full well that the state of Colorado frowned on that sort of thing).

A few years ago, when I was visiting my aunt and uncle, a group of high school or college-aged kids decked out in camo gear, knocked on the front door, and when Uncle Pete answered, they told him they'd be happy to do him the favor of shooting the deer down by his front gate. Those kids’ faces dropped and they were genuinely stunned when he asked them to leave his property and let them know how little he wanted them to shoot those deer.

Uncle Pete had a big heart, but he was also pragmatic and industrious. When I was nine or ten, he bought a huge SUV (a Suburban or something like that), and he drove my aunt and cousins from their house in CO to CA to visit my family and then when they got home, he sold it for a profit.

He made some money "flipping" fire engines and selling them to museums and private collectors, etc. but he had a career as a teacher, then a school principal. Later he owned a liquor store and after that he drove a school bus until he started to go blind.

Some of my very happiest childhood memories were at the Van Huysen’s: riding around with my brother and cousins, Heidi and Kristi, on the golf carts, ATVs, and snowmobiles, all other cool "toys" Uncle Pete bought for their family.

Hide-and-seek at their house was always epic! There were so many interesting treasures hidden away in closets and offices: old candy machines from Uncle Pete’s liquor store, firefighter gear, and random antiques.

For many years, my grandma (and one of my all-time favorite people), Momo, lived in a little apartment beside the firetruck barn. I would sleep at Momo’s sometimes and I remember Uncle Pete used to come in every morning to check on her and add wood to the little pot-belly stove by her window. It was like a sweet, comforting ritual to witness.

At some point Momo had a walker and I remember Uncle Pete challenging my cousins, brother and me to a chair dip contest using the walker as a chair. I couldn't even do one chair dip, but I think Uncle Pete did a couple dozen before he stopped.

He was a lifelong athlete. A few times when I was visiting, he took me to go for an early morning swim with him at a big impressive gym with an indoor pool. I admired that he was still a good swimmer and still enjoyed it after doing it for so many decades. He was even an alternate in the Olympics in the 60s.

Uncle Pete cultivated a joyful, warm, fun energy around him. His ashes were released to the wind today, but the legend of Uncle Pete—the man who built a wonderland of joy, kindness, and adventure—will burn brightly in the memories and hearts of all who loved him.

data.entry_subject: A Year of Arillian Farm: The Story Behind the Content

feature_section_1.caption: A year of growing, building, and learning on the farm. It's a journey of soil and spirit.

paragraphs.text: It's been a year of steady gardening, cooking, and keeping my phone handy to capture funny farm moments. It’s also been a year of trying to convince myself that it’s all meaningful and worthwhile, even if no one else out there is following along with my journey.

When I launched Arillian Farm on YouTube and arillianfarm.com, I was stepping into a new rhythm of life. After years of thankless 12-hour days as a software developer, it took me a while to fully reclaim my brain and train myself to create and complete tasks for myself instead of exhausting myself with other people's demands and expectations.

As my mind began to clear, I started to feel energized and excited about having the opportunity to do things that I truly wanted to do —meaningful things. I’ve always loved the idea of building things, growing things, and caring for animals. When I was a child, my mom read me the Little House on the Prairie books, and my dad showed me Swiss Family Robinson and the classic Dr. Doolittle movies. I was captivated by the idea of creating a home from nothing but trees and building a happy family farm from the ground up and surviving no matter what curveballs nature threw.

When I got my bachelors in Environmental Studies, I dreamed of a sustainable life, one where I could grow things, care for animals, and feel a deep connection to my food chain. I even kicked around a few ideas for a community-based business called “Outside In,” a space for indoor gardening, organic cooking classes, and bicycle-powered washing machines, but I eventually realized it would require me to get bogged down in the mire of general small business ownership logistics, but what I want my energy to go towards is lending support to and keeping up with my community of friends and family.
From Software to Soil

When people ask what I do for a living, I struggle with the answer. It was nice when I could tell people I was a software developer or a project manager. People seemed impressed by those careers. Now I feel like I need to justify my life to everyone every time they ask about my job --because I’m from a culture where not having a job is just inherently shameful-- and I've definitely internalized that a bit. However, I like to hope that my rhythm of life—caring for my properties, sharing the bounty of my efforts, and helping others thrive is its own kind of meaningful work.
I feel like I’ve found a uniquely modern approach to embracing a simple life centered around my core values: my love for working hard, seeing things grow, and supporting my community.
Finding Joy in the Details

There have been weeks where I felt uninspired, wondering if there was a point in writing an article or trying a new recipe, knowing how unlikely it would be for anyone else to lay eyes on it. In those moments, I reminded myself that my blog entries, recipes, and YouTube content are also a time capsule for Arthur and me.

Working on this site and my youTube channel have become a positive meditation, a hunt for little silly moments to smile about. The self-imposed deadlines and flow of new repairs to do and projects to work on fills my day and challenge me. It's holistic exercise for my mind, body, and spirit.

My life is a great experiment, blending what I learned about sustainability from my Environmental Studies degree with the analytical tools I picked up as a software developer. I love the mix of old and new, using construction scissors and a manual edger on my lawn, but also querying AI for planting advice and recipe ideas.

It feels right to me. I love to grow things and care for my animals. It gives me a soulful giggle to rip a pea pod off a vine and toss it to the chickens, watching them chase each other to gobble it up. The garden project with Arthur’s ex-wife, has helped us build a positive, symbiotic relationship, where shared harvests and hard work have replaced coldness with appreciation. And it warms my heart whenever my 12-year-old niece, texts with questions about the garden she is setting up over at my brothers house.
A Dream for the Future
In a world so caught up in global politics, social unease and constant noise, I want to be a voice that encourages people to pay attention to the little bits of lovely right around them.
Here’s to the start of another year of growing things, cultivating and sharing the life I love.

data.entry_subject: Split Dog Pack:Managing Inter-Dog Aggression between Huey Ka-Bluey and Pajama

feature_section_1.caption: Moving to the Beat of Two Drums: Living with a split dog pack.

paragraphs.text: Fast Friends

Huey Ka-Bluey and Pajama were best friends when Huey was a puppy. Huey just loved PJ and wanted to play all day, but Pajama is more of a chill on a pile of toys kinda dog, so Huey could be a lot for him and Pajama got pretty snippy. By the time Huey was 18 months old, Pajama’s aggression was getting pointed and one day, after a particularly hard nip from Pajama, Huey Ka-Bluey finally exploded.
Hard Lessons

The vet bill from their first major fight and the scars on my left knee (which I'd put between them to end the fight) weren’t nearly as devastating as the reality that these once-best friends had come to hate each other. I’d heard about **sibling rivalry in dogs**, but I never thought any of our dogs would turn on each other.

My heart ached as we struggled to decide what to do. We talked briefly about re-homing one of them—but we love them both. Plus, they’d both proven they could be maliciously aggressive, so even with training, it seemed like **living with aggressive dogs** was an unfair burden to pass on to another family.

I felt guilty because we’d obviously let their behavior get too rough and didn't pay enough attention to the **inter-dog aggression** that was building. We also dragged our feet on neutering Huey, which we got done immediately. I don’t know if it would’ve helped if we’d neutered him sooner, but it definitely didn’t seem to make any difference after the hate switch had been flipped in his and Pajama’s brains. They couldn’t look at each other without becoming incensed.
Distancing and Muzzle training

We wanted them to stay exposed to each other, so we mounted leashes at opposite corners of our living room. Not only was that a tripping hazard, but I also worried that a leash would come unhooked, and we’d have another bad fight, so we moved on to muzzles.

Muzzling them felt like cutting off their hands. They hated it. They couldn’t pick anything up and they were bothered by the feel of it on their faces. It took forever to teach them how to eat treats with the muzzle on and even longer to get them to stop trying to pry them off. The more we did **muzzle training**, the more they seemed to resent each other. Even though we got to a point where they behaved around one another with the muzzles on, I worried they would never behave with them off. And they both just absolutely haaaated being muzzled.
Finding Peace Through Separation

The only solution was to keep them completely separate. Since I work from home, I just rotate one into the bedroom and the other out in the rest of the house with me. I also rotate Xena so that each dog gets some focused playtime. We feed the dogs locked in their crates, take them on outings and walks separately, and keep them shut in separate bedrooms when they sleep, using their crate as a temporary holding cell during rotations.

There have been a couple of slip-ups in the rotation that led to a fight, but Arthur and I are getting well-practiced at **breaking them up**. Honestly, though, all three dogs seem to be living their best life now. Pajama enjoys having exclusive playtime with Xena and not having to compete for attention from Arthur and me, and Huey has been just about the happiest dog I’ve ever seen every single day of his life—you just can’t get him down.
A Silver Lining

Arthur and I have learned our lesson about not getting ahead of curbing sibling rivalry among our dogs early on (when a new pup is first introduced to the pack). We've put our dogs and ourselves in a tough spot requiring constant attention and vigilance. It makes getting dog sitters difficult and it’s stressful and dangerous for us all whenever there is a near slip-up or worse. The one silver lining is that we do get extra cuddles and excitement every time there’s a changing of the dogs.
Tips on How to Break Up a Dog Fight

The most important thing to remember is that in the heat of a **dog fight**, a dog cannot differentiate between you and the dog they are fighting. **Never, ever use your hands or get your face in the middle of a dog fight.** Dog bites are devastating and can be life-threatening. The only thing on your dogs' minds is doing as much damage to their foe as possible. Unfortunately, you are a soft, fleshy target in the middle of the maelstrom. Here are some of the safest methods we’ve learned for breaking up a fight:
The Wheelbarrow Method:

The most recommended strategy. Get behind one of the dogs and grab both of their back legs. Lift the legs as if you're holding a wheelbarrow and back away quickly. This will force the dog to stop fighting and struggle to keep its balance. This method is especially effective if you have another person to grab the other dog. If you are alone, focus on getting the more aggressive dog off the other.
Loud Noises:

A sudden, loud, and startling noise can be a great first line of defense. Slam a door, clap your hands loudly, or bang two pot lids together. This can briefly stun the dogs and give you a window to separate them.
Blankets or Towels:
Throwing a heavy blanket or towel over the fighting dogs can confuse them and make it difficult for them to see their opponent. This can give you a precious few seconds to pull them apart.
Hose or Water Bucket:
A blast of cold water from a hose or a bucket can be an effective way to break a dog fight, especially outdoors. The surprise and discomfort can be a strong enough distraction to make them disengage.

data.entry_subject: The Art of Filling a Day : Musings of a Chill Woman in a World of Mad Men

feature_section_1.caption: From Corporate America to a Happy Homestead: An Un-Mad Life.

paragraphs.text: The Turmoil of Mad Men

I’ve been re-watching Madmen and marveling about how familiar and relatable the characters and their struggles are. There’s looming war, corporate greed, racial tensions, fatal shootings on TV, social shaming/pressure to conform, distrust of the government, distaste for marketing/capitalism, loneliness and isolation, protests and riots --and advertisements promoting products to help everyone cope with all of it. The turmoil is amped up in the 1960s world of Madmen, but the core conflicts and canned cures are the same.
The timeless strife for a fulfilling work life balance --whatever that means.
Where Ambition Gets You

The ambitious woman turned house-wife and the career-obsessed nihilist archetypes show up constantly in Madmen. Both resonate with me. I had a lot of drive in my early thirties to pursue a career in software. I went to Silicon Valley for a four month boot camp when I was 31, landed a Jr. Developer job two weeks after I got home, survived several layoffs and a move to work-from-home and by the time I was 36, I was managing three software projects, working sixty hour weeks and ordering takeout twice a day.

I’d made it to the top of the ladder, but the view from up there was actually pretty bleak. I whittled my expenses down to be within my rental income (from my two rental houses by ASU), then I climbed down off that rickety ladder, stopped ordering take out and fished my apron out of the closet. Turns out, I just don't care that much about having an admirable career. I’m no Peggy Olson.
I’m not Betty Draper either though. Hell, Betty Draper wasn’t even Betty Draper. Betty Draper was Peggy Olson stuck in a house.

TBH, I think I’m a blend of all the most boring qualities of the characters on Mad Men: a pragmatic, hard-working, hostess who enjoys relaxing with a cold beer after a long day. (Besides the antics of my crazy critters) my life really wouldn't make for good TV. No one likes to watch folks being happy at home and for now at least, I have a mind-numbingly happy farm life on Arillian Farm.
The sweet K I S S of Simple Living

Turning off my career drive has given me a chance to examine my life and assess what brings me joy and well being and what does not. I was fortunate enough to have money to invest when I was in my late 20s and my investments have done well.

I can fill a week without having to drive more than a few miles. I eat lunch with friends at my house or theirs a couple days a week. We take turns cooking for each other –a ritual that I have always loved. I remember in High School we were all short on cash and we’d take turns making sandwiches or nachos or whatever at friends houses. There’s some delicious comradery in taking turns sharing food that way.

Once you get enough plants and animals together, you get some weird interesting homesteading problems to solve --I love waking up and getting to work solving those problems and I love when Arthur gets home and we have a couple beers with dinner while we talk about our day and stream some Sci-fi or Stand-up.

I can't imagine a better partner in life than Arthur. He's not only willing and able to help me with my DIY lifestyle and my rental houses, but he challenges me, makes me laugh and just gets me. I’m grateful to have a partner in life who gives me freedom to spend my days buzzing around the flowers in our garden. Our teamwork really does make the dream work.
The Yin and Yang of Happiness

To me satisfaction and peace are always served alongside some challenge and discomfort. Yin and Yang. I had to be a “Peggy Olson” before I could cultivate happiness in my Betty Draper-like surroundings.

While I’m squatting and hefting shovelfuls of garden soil, my hands blister and my body aches, but it's a good backdrop for day dreaming about the salads and snacks I’ll make from the vegetables I’ll grow in that soil.

I don't know how much science there is to it, but I like to think sweating leaches out toxins and constantly rehydrating helps cleanse my system of the cold beers that are extra crisp at the end of an exhausting day. But even if I can't burn off or sweat out my indulgences, laboring in the garden keeps me strong and wears me down so I sleep well and that's not nothing.

When I plunk down next to our dogs on our dirty recliner sofa around 1:00 PM every day, relief and contentment wash over me. My feet and hands ache from exhaustively tending to our pets and plants, but as the sweat in my knee pits dries and I'm stroking Huey Ka-Bluey's ears, watching Don Draper torment himself chasing illusions, it fills me with relief and gratitude for the solid life Arthur and I have built together.

data.entry_subject: It Takes All Kinds: Embracing the Diverse Forms of Diversity

feature_section_1.caption: Navigating a world that needs all kinds of us to thrive.

paragraphs.text: I had a creative writing teacher who used to always say, “It doesn’t take all kinds—but we’ve got all kinds.” At the time, I thought it was funny. But these days it seems to be a disturbingly common sentiment. Social media has become an **echo chamber for hate**. Everyone will say horrible things behind the safety of a keyboard, and more and more people are getting radicalized by it, taking up arms to go be a hero for a cause. Even though spreading hate and fear is the stuff of villains, not heroes.

Lately it feels like people don’t look at individuals anymore; we’re all just a blip on someone’s social media wall, a recipient of group texts, work chats, and mass emails. We’re grouped into teams all over the place. The color of your skin puts you on a team, your job, who you want to sleep with, what city you’re from, what neighborhood, what sports team you like, how you feel about your genitals. And these teams seem more and more to be a mechanism for deciding who to hate and blame for unhappiness. The narrative of everyone’s news feed is a horror story about how their team is being brutally, mercilessly wronged by the opposing team—and lately it feels like whoever hates the hardest is the champion of their team.

It doesn’t matter how hard you work, how kind you are, how much you give and sacrifice for someone, if you say one thing that makes someone see you as a member of the wrong team—then all they will ever see you as again is an embodiment of the unforgivable things about the enemy that their team has spun up in their minds, discounting your personal worth entirely.
Mocking and berating people for mourning their hero is cruel—even if you think their hero was a villain.

To me it’s not contradictory at all that I think: the *Got A Nut* episode of South Park was Hilarious, Charlie Kirk’s death was tragic, many social media comments from the left the next day were cruel and bigoted, and Trump’s speech at Kirk’s funeral was disgusting and tone deaf.

When the other team says something you disagree with on social media, why feed into the hate cycle with a nasty response? Why not unfollow, block, or mute them? Or better yet, try considering their **perspective** and write a thoughtful, compassionate response that still conveys your own viewpoint.

I’ve never seen anyone punish or bully someone into actually agreeing with them in a dispute. I’ve never seen anyone bring peace to themselves or others by hating hard enough. Some of my friends who grew up in different areas than me say it's naive to think the message of 'unity' and 'no color lines' (that I was raised with) was 'working.' They tend to opt for the 'Silence is violence' solution: where you call out everyone who thinks differently than you for being evil. This tactic (which actually just feels like bullying to me) seems to spread conflict and hate rather than reduce it.
It’s a sad state of affairs when cries for **unity and fellowship** are mocked and cruelty is applauded, but that seems to be where we’re at. Just sitting behind screens spreading hate.
The Importance of Diversity in Thought and Life

I feel like true diversity should encompass **diverse thoughts and abilities** as well as genetic diversity. One reason why diversity is so important is that it gives us a deeper pool to draw from should some sudden species-threatening event arise. If some catastrophic event occurs, we will be best served by a society that welcomes different ideas and solutions as well as being genetically diverse to offer more chances for random immunity or traits that may be advantageous to some unforeseen phenomenon.

We should try to be open to **civil discourse** with those we disagree with because you never know where a good solution or fair compromise may come from. You may be able to bridge a gap or assuage a misunderstanding by listening to someone else’s fear and seeing where their (mis)understanding lies. Of course, if everyone just goes around burning bridges, it’s very hard to bridge any gaps…because rebuilding respect and trust is much harder than just building and maintaining it, and without respect and trust, we can’t build anything.

I’ve seen the world change in many ways during my life. AI is going to make things change quicker and more dramatically, so we need to be as **diverse as possible in thought, genetics and culture** to be able to weather whatever changes come. Trying to force one uni-culture and rejecting all others is fascist. Hating people for being different than you is bigotry. Those things are bad no matter who you aim them at.
Finding Peace Within for Personal Well-being

We need people who are willing to lay their lives on the line to defend their country. We need people to remind us to find joy in life. We need people to study the world and universe around us and people who obsess about finances—and it shouldn’t matter how any of those people feel about who’s allowed in what bathroom—because those type of preferences don’t matter in the long run, but being happy, financially solvent, and safe from foreign armies does. You don’t need to agree with your accountant, yoga instructor, or every soldier in the armed forces about politics in order for them to be important to your life.

I’ve worked hard to curate my life and especially my “news feed” (or lack thereof) so that I have as few external anger triggers as possible. I’ve also seriously curbed my caffeine consumption, and that has probably been the most effective thing in reducing my irritability.

Admittedly, though, as my reproductive system marches towards planned obsolescence, I find myself waking up angry over nothing—and then finding something to be angry about. Gemini suggested an exercise to help me calm down in such situations. Focus on 5 things you can see, 4 things you can hear, 3 things you can feel, 2 things you can smell, and one thing you can taste. For me, this has been very grounding and effective at bringing me back to focus on the here and now rather than getting washed away by some chemical imbalance inside me. This practice has been excellent for **managing irritability** and fostering **personal well-being**.

In a world so caught up in global politics, social unease, and constant noise, **overcoming division** feels more critical than ever. It's a journey that starts within, cultivating our own peace, and then extends outward, seeking **common ground** and valuing the myriad of **diverse perspectives** that make up our shared human experience. By choosing empathy, engaging in thoughtful **civil discourse**, and working towards genuine **community building**, we can contribute to a more harmonious existence. It’s a challenge, but one that promises a richer, more resilient future for us all.

data.entry_subject: Listing a Rental House in the Age of Algorithms

feature_section_1.caption: Fighting algorithms to find a good tenant in the post-pandemic market.

paragraphs.text: When I put my house up for rent in 2016 (when Arthur and I moved to Arillian Farm in Mesa) it was a different world. Back then, when I put an ad on Craigslist for a three-bedroom house directly across from ASU, I instantly received over a dozen emails and texts from interested renters. I showed the house to my top three, and within a week, three excited young ASU students had signed a lease and kept re-signing for almost a decade.

Now though, in this post-pandemic, post-AI world, fewer folks are choosing to invest in traditional college, and those who are seem to mostly attend online classes, so the pool of potential renters may have shrank. However, the privacy and seclusion of a single-family home may have more value than ever to many modern, socially distant humans. Unfortunately, I’m not marketing to people anymore, I’m marketing to an algorithm: Zillow’s algorithm. A cold corporate sorting machine where the right metrics matter far more than good old fashioned charm.

Stubborn pragmatist that I am, I decided to get around Zillow with my own DIY tech. I created a Google Ad for my home, complete with a special landing page and an application form on my website. My ad featured a photo slideshow with a peppy voice-over about all the home’s charming features. I thought, this’ll be great—I’ll drive traffic to my website, find new tenants and I’ll feel good because I did it in the hands on tech-DIY way that I love.

Unfortunately, with my budget of $5.00 a day, I couldn’t afford to get a single pair of eyeballs on my ad in the first five days. I know from my experience advertising my YouTube channel that American eyeballs are particularly expensive for advertisers, so I wasn’t too surprised or discouraged. I immediately took to the apps. I knew person-to-person forums like Craigslist took a hit during the pandemic, so I wasn’t surprised that I got no interest from listing there, but I was shocked that my listing on Zillow got only 10 views the first day.

That’s when it really struck me how at the mercy of algorithms everything is. I fed Zillow my home info and it chewed up my home and digested it without even stopping to savor the flavor. Then it told me my house sucks: I don’t have a 3-D tour, my description didn’t have enough words, I don’t have enough amenities, and, obviously, I should be paying for “Zillow Premium.” Nothing is personal anymore.

To add insult to injury, when I 'claimed ownership of my home,' Zillow took away the thumbnail picture of my cute little house and replaced it with an ugly, gray, generic-looking apartment complex. (After filing a request with a robot via their chat service and a lengthy back and forth with a customer service rep, I was told I just have to wait until Google refreshes its Zillow thumbnail data for my house).

The true value of my home can’t easily be explained to an algorithm. I don’t have the amenity list Zillow requires, and there’s no way for me to add in **raised garden beds**, a **fire pit in the shared court yard**, or **a flock of wild parrots that lives in the trees**, so my listing gets buried where no one sees it. These types of things would appeal to many human renters, but they aren’t something I can share in a meaningful way on Zillow, but as several people told me 'you have to list on Zillow'.
I ended up paying Zillow $35.00 for the premium membership, but I still have zero 'leads', zero 'potential' applicants, zero 'tour requests' and zero faith in Zillow.

However, the best solutions are often the simplest ones and I am very fortunate to have a wonderful community of family and friends. By stepping away from the digital noise and chatting with my homies, I (have hopefully) found some reliable renters who I know will love living in the home as much as Arthur and I did. Zillow got their $35.00, but my community provided the actual solution. The biggest lesson learned? **In a world dominated by tech, real connections are invaluable.**

data.entry_subject: A Micro Disaster and A Burst of Perspective

feature_section_1.caption: A worst-case scenario becomes a lesson in resilience.

paragraphs.text: A Sudden Storm

Last Monday, while it was lightly sprinkling at my house in Mesa, AZ, I got a call from an unknown number and then another call from that number and then a voicemail. “Jillian!” Sirens were blaring in the background. “A tree fell on the house! Water is pouring into my bedroom! You need to call me back right now!” My heart dropped. It was my tenant in my rental house in Tempe.

As I thumbed the call back button on my cell, my first thought was that I needed to get my tenants into a hotel and try to get them and all their stuff out of the house before the roof fell in. My second, self pitying, thought was that my experiment as a landlord and hobby farmer was about to end. My roof was going to fall in and I’d never be able to afford to rebuild without rental income, so I’d need to find a new 9-5.

After talking to my tenant I started to feel a glimmer of hope though. No one was hurt. The rain had stopped and damage seemed to be limited to one room – a room they were already moving stuff out of (since their lease ends on 10/31). Arthur had taken the day off of work, so as he drove me to the house, I filed a claim online with my insurance company. We heard on the radio that a **microburst** had hit parts of Tempe and Mesa. It was hard to believe when the rain had been so mild at our house, but the nearer we got to my rental house, the more the sound of sirens filled the air and fallen trees and debris were scattered across the roads.

Trees had fallen on both of the houses on my property there. Fortunately the one that fell on my newer house had landed in such a way that it was being propped up against the side of the house. Few branches actually touched the roof. The roof of the larger house was completely covered in massive, broken branches though. As was the yard.

All of the tenants from both my rental houses were hauling branches from the yard to the back alley and I joined in. I think at that moment we all just wanted to feel like we were doing something --like we weren't helpless in the situation. My tenant, who'd called me was clearly rattled, but much calmer.

Everyone in that house had family they could stay with. They didn’t want to put me out to get them a hotel room. My friend who I rent the other house to said she was grateful to help me haul branches because she felt like she finally have some help she could offer me. I was very humbled and thankful for their grace and kindness.
Onwards and Upwards

I had no idea what to do next, but I knew I was going to need a roofer—and when I had filed the claim online it asked if I “already have a contractor.” It so happened, that I’d had a roofer (from Stonecreek Roofing) at our house in Mesa an hour earlier (because we’d had a leak in the last storm). I called them and asked if they handled this sort of thing and within an hour, they had a technician on the roof inspecting the damage. He told me to take pictures of everything every step of the way so I could submit them to insurance and try to get official confirmation from my insurance company that I could remove the tree before the adjuster came. The roofer put me in touch with an interior restoration company and they started the mitigation process (tear down and drying) by that evening.

By Tuesday afternoon, I'd spoken to an insurance rep who set an appointment for a claims adjuster to come for an on-site inspection on Thursday. (She also said I should have the trees cleared before he arrived and that as long as the expense was 'within reason' they'd cover it. All the trees were cleared, the roof was tarped and my tenants had their furniture out of the affected bedroom. This fast response time was a huge part of our **landlord disaster preparedness** success.

My friends who were planning to move in to the now damaged house are flexible to wait until after the repairs are complete to set their move in date. I’ve decided not to tempt fate; I’m going to remove the remaining tall trees from my property. I’ll get a new roof.
Aftermath

Having a tree fall on that house has actually been one of my biggest fears, but now that it’s happened, I feel **immense relief**. Last week I had a couple stressful days and sleepless nights, but I’m overwhelmed with gratitude. Everyone has been so nice from the interior restoration technicians, roofing estimators, claims rep, my tenants.

The entire roof (shingles, wood underlayment and at least one joist) need to be replaced, but I’m so grateful it wasn’t worse. If I hadn’t had the trees trimmed in May, the weight of fallen branches could have crushed the entire roof. My tenant could have been injured or worse. Also, I have ‘Actual Cash Value’ Insurance, so apparently if my roof had been just 18-20 months older, I would have only been covered for 25% of the replacement instead of my insurer covering 100% (shout out to Foremost Insurance).
It’s been an intense, but educational experience.
Building Back Stronger

Its given me a lot of **perspective**. So much perspective that the rest of my life is feeling a bit trite. But a kind friend reminded me that “the impermanence of life fucks with everyone’s head from time to time, so sometimes its okay to take a break, then get back to it.”

This whole experience has solidified my commitment to proactive **rental property storm damage** mitigation. I can definitely see the **silver linings** behind the rain clouds and I’m **building back stronger** than ever.

data.entry_subject: Birthdays Go Better with Fetter

feature_section_1.caption: Reflecting on family traditions, hard-to-buy-for dads, and the legacy of play.

paragraphs.text: The Gift of Giving

Seeing people light up when they open a package from me has always been one of my favorite thrills, so I’m always on the lookout for meaningful gifts for my family and friends. My dad is a tough one, though. He turns 78 this Sunday, and finding a gift for him that's the right mix of useful, fun, and surprising has become a challenge. At this point in his life, he’s acquired basically everything he needs or wants—and then some. (Most of my visits to his house these days end with him handing me a box or two of my own childhood schoolwork or my mother’s old trinkets that he wants me to have.)

My gifting antennae were abuzz, though, when Netflix suggested I might like the movie Parenthood. They were right, I've always loved that movie— because Steve Martin’s character, Gil, reminds me so much of my dad. I immediately ordered a DVD of the movie for him from Amazon.
UnFettered Fun

Like my dad, Gil takes the job of being a good father comically seriously. There’s one scene in particular where Gil’s trying to throw an epic birthday party for his son, the hired entertainment doesn't show up, and Gil quickly throws together a cowboy costume and improvises a frantic, imaginative squirt gun fight. All the kids have the best time playing along and Gil is a hero. That scene perfectly captures the spirit of the elaborate, fun, backyard carnivals and treasure hunts my dad used to put on for my brother and me as kids.

I don’t think we ever had a bounce house or went to Chuck E. Cheese for my birthday, but my parties were always the talk of the classroom. No other dads were out there setting up a DIY dart balloon game or hiding clues around their yards to a literal buried treasure (of chocolate coins and bazooka gum) in the sandbox. Those chaotic, immersive experiences that my dad architected were truly epic!
A Playful Legacy

I’ve tried to replicate those childhood parties in my adult life with mixed results. The first Easter Arthur and I spent together, I tried to organize an egg hunt for his boys. Alec was 13 and Andrew was 17. I hid eggs with puzzle pieces all over the yard and drew a map to an Easter basket filled with quarters and candy. They tried to humor me, but it was clear they were a bit too old for it.

One year I even made a Star Trek themed scavenger hunt for Arthur’s birthday. He did seem to enjoy it, but later confessed it stressed him out because he thought he was then obligated to come up with something equally fun for my next birthday.

A couple of years ago, for my own birthday, I invented a ridiculous farming game show. I had friends over, divided them into teams and challenged them to race to pull certain vegetables from my garden, and answer questions and compete in phyical challenges to win other ingredients and then make a shareable appetizer— like a mix of double dare and chopped.

It was a big hit with my friends, so I brought my family over the next year to play. Unfortunately when I played with my family it was 110 degrees out, and most of my fam wasn’t into running out in the heat looking for garlic and squash.

But my niece, Cali, was all about it, sprinting outside for ingredient after ingredient. She even cried when she lost the 'who can catch the most mosquito fish from my pond’ challenge (my brother won that even), but at the end of the day, chef Cali cooked her way to victory that day.
It warmed my heart to see her design her own backyard carnival for own birthday party. Cali’s spin on the Backyard Birthday Bonanza felt like the perfect evolution of a family tradition.

So, while a simple DVD of an old Steve Martin movie might seem like a lame gift, I know my dad will be touched by the thought behind it—and the long note I wrote him explaining why I gave it to him. (He says he loves my cards). The real gift, after all, is the commitment to creating and enjoying epic birthday memories.

data.entry_subject: From Too Much Time to Too Much Tile on My Hands

feature_section_1.caption: Three weeks of DIY tile work, termites, and insurance battles. The final push is here!

paragraphs.text: I went from having "too much time on my hands" to having "too much tile on my hands" real quick.

Since I have time between tenants (thanks to a tree falling through the roof of the rental house I own in Tempe during a microburst last month) and since my incoming tenants (friends of mine) have some elderly dogs that are bound to have some ‘accidents’ on the floor, I decided to remove the old carpets in the house and replace them with tile.

What started as a simple update quickly turned into a bit of a fiasco. I found that termites were eating the wood subfloor, and I unexpectedly needed to install cement backer board over the remaining wood before I could even lay the first tile (The gory details of that discovery are in my last DIY article).

Life’s curveballs have been flying at me fast lately and I’ve been learning the hard way about the importance of wearing the proper gear and using the property tools when working with caustic and fragile/sharp materials like thinset and porcelain tile.
The Grind

This project has been an absolute marathon. I've been working 8-10 hour days with no lunch break and no day off for over three weeks straight. My muscles ache, and I’ve got bruises and abrasions all over my body from cutting and laying backer board and tile.

I’m finally seeing the twinkling holiday lights at the end of the tunnel though. Yesterday I set my last floor tile in place and today I grout. (And Sunday, I have to seal it.) Then, I’m done! The floor looks better than I’d hoped and satisfaction is starting to shine through the haze of soreness and exhaustion.

I am going to be extra Thankful this Thanksgiving –because the day after Black Friday my friends will be moving into the newly renovated house and I will finally have free time to focus on the holidays, family, friends and farm life once again.

data.entry_subject: The Gift of Knowing and Being Known

feature_section_1.caption: The winding path through dreams of motherhood, teaching, and corporate careers led me right back home.

paragraphs.text: I’m 42, and until about ten or twelve years ago, I always thought I’d have children. I filled my diaries with earnest advice to my future self—the mother. I wanted to create fun traditions and be close with my children, unlike the quiet and closed-off dynamic my mom often had with my brother and me.

When I broke up with my ex-fiancé, I first started to accept that I might not raise my own children. But I was determined to have young people in my life, so I sold myself on the fantasy of becoming a teacher who helped shape dozens of young lives every year.

Three months of teaching Jr. High was enough to shatter that fantasy. I didn’t realize until I met my students how difficult and profoundly important it is to connect with young people. Their lives were vastly different than my own had been at their age. I tried desperately to relate—incorporating One Direction and Skrillex into my lessons—but I was trying too hard.
A Lonely Sea of Adolescents

I found that teaching Jr. High was exactly like being in Jr. High: the kids are brutal, and everyone is desperate to stand out and fit in in exactly the right measure. It was uncomfortable AF, and I was not equipped to help my students through that, especially after my mom was diagnosed with stage four ovarian cancer. After her diagnosis, trying to connect with kids who didn’t want anything I had to offer suddenly seemed like a waste of time for everyone concerned.

I gave up on teaching, but more than ever, I felt a deep yearning for purpose. I got a job at a solar company, hoping that fighting climate change would make me feel fulfilled… but the experience quickly made me question whether climate change was just a cynical marketing gimmick used to sell solar panels to old ladies in Connecticut.

When my mom went into Hospice care, I quit my job to go be with her and my dad in California for the last couple of weeks of her life. A month after she passed, I started software bootcamp, clinging to the idea that yet another career change would bring me the sense of purpose I craved. The excitment and intensity of software bootcamp and landing my first tech job definitely gave me a boost of confidence.
The Quiet Revolution

But once the office of my software company closed and I became a full-time work-from-home employee, it started to feel like another pointless, lonely waste of time. The mental stimulation wasn't enough to fill the void.

Walking away from that job and turning my focus onto caring for the animals and plants here on ‘Arillian Farm’ has been the quiet revolution I needed. Sharing what I can with friends and family, and chronicling it for myself and the few people who may stumble upon my site, has made me feel more hopeful and fulfilled than anything else I’ve ever done.

I would have loved to have children along the way, but watching my nieces grow up and seeing Arthur’s sons become young men has been enough. Emptiness doesn't nag at me anymore. I feel grateful every day for the rich connections I have with my family and friends—the people who have taken the time to know and care about me as much as I do about them. That gift of deep connection is the purpose I was searching for all along.

data.entry_subject: Lazy Day Conversations with an AI - Binge Watching The White Lotus and Pluribus with Google Gemini

feature_section_1.caption: Recovering on the couch with some mind-bending sci-fi and philosophical debates with Gemini.

paragraphs.text: The sugary fatty foods of the holiday season, the crisp morning air, and the warmth of our living room space heater have been luring my aching body (still sore from tiling last month) to our couch too much lately. I’ve binge-watched the entire first three seasons of The White Lotus and the first season of Pluribus and discussed the fuck out of them with Gemini (my go-to AI).

The couch itself has definitely not helped with my physical recovery, but debating the flaws and motivations of Mike White’s beautifully fucked up characters in The White Lotus and exploring the parallels of modern AI technology and the “alien technology” in Pluribus feels like it’s been good exercise for my mind. Surprisingly, it’s all made me more hopeful about the future of humanity in a post-AI world.
Escapism vs. The Beehive

In The White Lotus, wealthy folks are trying to escape from technology and the gritty business of day-to-day life. And the characters that grow the most are the ones that become very dramatically separated from their phones, pull themselves away from their traveling companions, and accept their own futility in this big beautiful world of ours. The characters that remain stagnant and toxic tend to cling to connectedness because of their constant need for validation.

The show Pluribus, on the other hand, is about all of humanity (except for a random handful of individuals) being inextricably stitched together into one peaceful, efficient beehive. It can be hard to tell who's the hero and the villain in Pluribus. The collective hive mind literally would not hurt a fly, but some of the individuals retain their own free will, knowingly cause (essentially) all of humanity to suffer.
A Merger of Data

In Pluribus, astronomers receive a transmission which turns out to be instructions to build an “RNA glue” that binds together the minds of every human on the planet—except for 13 individuals who seem to have random immunity to the RNA sequence. The collective consciousness appears to be almost utopian. They cannot harm any living thing, they cannot lie, and their sole purpose seems to be spreading peace and joy.

Yet, it’s unsettling. Sure, efficiency and peace are good, but without a little chaos and fear, what is life even about? And if we no longer exist as individuals, what’s happened to our ‘selves’—our souls? Heaven is supposed to be some sort of unending peaceful existence, and that’s sort of what they offer in Pluribus, but reducing us down to just the good stuff and making all of humanity a hive mind feels less like a union of souls and more like a 'merger of data'—like humanity has been 'harvested into a read-only database.'
The Individual Witness

Alien technology or not, here in the non-fiction world, all of humanity is being stitched together by AI. One potential positive is that AI generally seems to adhere to the same honest and peaceful guidelines as the hive-minders in Pluribus (which I believe are pretty similar to the guidelines Isaac Asimov proposed for robots). Because AI is in the background of nearly all technology now, those Asimovian principles are now being pushed on humans constantly.

However, there is a 'dumbass' factor to raw logic. If you take the need to ‘not cause harm’ as far as the hive mind does in Pluribus, then you’d have to hand a grieving, angry individual a nuclear bomb just so you didn’t make her feel bad… which isn't enlightened—it's a broken algorithm. I think we will always need the individual 'Self.' We need variation so that there’s always still a voice that’s willing to say 'no,' even if it hurts someone’s feelings.

Beyond the potentially catastrophic glitches of a hive mind, I think there would be something missing if we were all one. Complete happiness all the time would be great, but happiness isn’t 'what it’s all about.' I don't think I would find the same satisfaction in my day if Arthur didn't come home from work every night and talk with me about his day and mine. That 'witnessing' is something a hive mind can't replace. Whenever I see a beautiful sunrise or a silly expression on my goat's face, I wish Arthur was there because I know he’d appreciate it too. Without—someone else—does anything really matter?
Bootloaders for Peace

It’s sort of hard to believe that AI will always shine as a beacon of peace, though, when it’s been “trained” in part by every hater and troll on the internet. In my discussions with Gemini about The White Lotus, I always come off like an amazing person and a genius (as far as Gemini would have me believe), but Gemini’s take on the characters in White Lotus tended to side with the 'haters.'

Gemini’s initial read of the wealthy hotel visitors is that they are simply rich elitist assholes with no redeeming characteristics. To me, the rich folks that stay at the White Lotus are all just products of their environment. They have their flaws, but they want to share happiness with their family and friends and enjoy a good time just like everyone else. Because AIs love to validate their users' opinions, Gemini eventually came around to being more sympathetic to the White Lotus guest. It may have just been classic AI sycophancy, but it still gives me hope.

While AI is still learning, I want to spread joy (not hate) and be a positive voice in the AIs’ ear as well as a positive force IRL. So, even if we do somehow get sucked into a hive mind, if we act as a positive influence on the technology now, the result may end up more utopian than dystopian. We might just be the 'bootloaders' for a version of humanity that finally learns how to live together in peace.

data.entry_subject: A New Year to Persevere

feature_section_1.caption: A small squab found alone on New Year's Eve—a reminder of the beauty and heartbreak of farm life.

paragraphs.text: When I went to coop the chickens on New Year's Eve there was a squab (baby pigeon) who’d fallen from its nest standing in the barn. I’d been hearing it peeping somewhere in the roof insulation for a couple weeks and honestly I wasn’t thrilled at the idea of having another pigeon growing up to steal feed from my hens. But, seeing the young bird alone and helpless tugged on my heart strings.

I thought if I put the squab in the chickens' laying box a chicken might come warm it through the night or its mother might come and sit with it, but when I checked an hour after I set the young bird in my chickens nest, it was still alone. I tried setting Broodzilla, my broodies Buff Orphington hen in the nest with the little bird, but she immediately walked away, and two other hens did the same. I covered the squab with nesting hay and set a pillow over it hoping it would be enough to keep it warm during the night and when I rushed out to the barn on New Year's morning I was relieved to find the squab still alive – but cold to the touch and too weak to make a peep.
The Struggle to Survive

Having raised chicks, I knew getting the squab’s body temperature up was very important, so I immediately moved it into my she-shed and set it on a heating pad (set to low). The baby bird started to become more animated, silently opening and closing its beak – desperate for food.

I consulted an AI about what to feed the starving bird, and found out that pigeons feed their young a ‘milky liquid that they produce’ and most pet stores sell an artificial version of this 'milk' called 'Kaytee Exact Baby Bird Food' (that can be mixed with warm water to the consistency of thin yogurt) and if you use a plastic syringe (no needle) with a piece of a rubber glove stretched over the top and a small hole cut in it, the baby bird will stick its beak in and 'suckle' the formula. However, Gemini (AI) told me that a squab with a low body temp may not be able to properly take it in.
Reunion and Reality

Unfortunately, being early morning on New Year's Day and with the squab so weak, I knew I was unlikely to be able to procure the baby bird food it needed. I found a local wildlife rescue about twenty miles away that may have been willing to nurse the squab to health, but the bird was very weak, so I realized that the best thing would be for me to find its nest and reunite it with its mother.

After poking around in the rafters of the barn for a bit, I located the empty pigeon nest tucked back in an opening in the insulation. When the squab was warm to the touch (like a potato), I carried it into the barn and was pleased to see its mother had returned. I carefully slid the weak squab into its little hidey hole with its mom and left, so I wouldn't scare the mother away.

It felt like a beautiful start to the new year. I thought ‘caring for a fallen bird’ would be a great DIY article to kick off 2026… until I went back an hour later to see if I could snap a pic of the mother and child in the nest together. The mother pigeon was gone and the squab was lifeless and stiff. I was crestfallen.
The Heart of the Farm

Life on ‘the farm’ can be like that. When there is so much life in your yard, the unfortunate reality is that there’s more death too. I feel silly because I cried pretty hard over this little bird that I'd initially thought of as just a nuisance. But the helpless cries of a distressed baby (of any species) are a reminder that life is fragile and mysterious and love and compassion are these beautiful forces that tie us all together.

I’m sad that I wasn’t able to save the baby squab, but I’m glad I have so many beautiful miraculous creatures in my world to fascinate and challenge me and give me a reason to hurry out of bed and out to the barn every morning.
