paragraphs.text: POV JENNA
6 - SEND-OFF
NEW EARTH - HOPEFUL MOUNTAINTOP

“And—” Diego cups his hands around his mouth as he stands at the edge of Hopeful Mountaintop, shouting at the vibrant peach sunrise.“—a massive, solid-aluminum Parabolic Mirror Dish that’s four point five meters in diameter and zero point eight meters deep, with a highly-polished interior surface and a reinforced rear structural ribbing frame for scaffold mounting.” Diego lowers his hands from his mouth and scans the horizon. The only sound is the faint whistle of the frigid wind.

Turning away from the sunrise, Diego strides across the plateau towards the fifty of us packed together by the edge of the origin crater. We huddle against the massive, charred flank of the adult Dino Nugget, crackling shards of mirrored lightning glass in heaps around us. The beast’s colossal ribcage is still giving off a faint, smoky warmth, radiating heat through the granite beneath our bare feet, while its meat warms our bellies from inside.

For me, last night’s meal felt more like a nightmarish dinner theater than a celebratory feast though: chasing greasy meat with slurps of tepid rain water while The Gleam and his eleven companions descended down the cliff.
All the while, Diego barked at us, “Talk while you eat.” “Get with your committee.” “Figure out what two items each of you want me to list off for Hyperspear.”

Every one of the Hopefuls that followed The Gleam off the mountaintop was more valuable than any item Hyperspear will materialize for us. We should have tried to convince them to stay, but I guess Diego was right, we don’t have a single second to spare on someone who can’t put survival above pride.
I sigh, staring with half-hearted hope at the sky, my eyes flicking between Diego and the pastel horizon.

Diego’s a few yards from us when a blinding, silent white-blue light vaporizes a fifty-foot radius in the forest several miles North of Hopeful Mountaintop. A shrieking tsunami of terrified creatures stampede away from the ionization event in all directions.
Then, the sky catches up.

A deafening, metallic CRACK rips through the air, swallowing up the jungle screams. The granite floor shudders and a violent, hot gust of wind slams across the plateau, whipping my shaggy hair into my face. It instantly reverses, transforming into a freezing vacuum draft that sucks loose ash straight toward the northern horizon.
Coughing and sputtering, the Hopefuls around me erupt into uncontrolled glee.

“Look at that St Elmo’s Fire!” Xenia exclaims in awe, from somewhere in the crowd. "Hyperspear is firing an ionization beam from its spaceship to literally tear the molecules in the air apart and forge our assets from raw elements!”
“Isn’t this amazing?” Luke pulls me into a side hug. “And I think my dad nailed the whole list!”

“Yup.” I stiffen up, tugging my hairy tube dress up and forcing a smile. “I heard him call out the diamond sewing needle and the cast-Iron Flat Iron I picked too.” My mind fills with memories of lavender steam and Myka’s face. My last innocently happy memory.
“That iron’ll be a great anvil for welding.” Luke grins. “Or a weapon in a pinch.”

“Yeah.” I pull away from Luke, sidling away from the gleeful Hopefuls, away from the beam of energy in the sky. I trot across the cold granite, hugging my bare shoulders for warmth, as I find myself a quiet palace at the edge of the plateau.

Behind me, the crowd chatters with unanimous joy. The weary hours of discussion and rehearsing paid off. Some all powerful genie in the sky is dropping off all the non-living objects our newly-minted hearts could ever desire.
We’ll have a fantastic set of supplies to get started on New Earth. I shiver. But will any of that actually help me to rebuild the happiness I had with Myka.
Slumping down onto the cool granite, I roll onto my back letting out a meditative hum as I try to focus on the swirl of colors illuminating across the sky.

“Jenna?” Xenia calls from outside the cave. “Jenna!” Xenia’s bare feet slap the rock floor as she jogs over, crouching down beside me, her face smeared with last night’s dino grease. “I know you’re still mad at me —Cut this Glitch loose!” Xenia’s left eye spasms and she squirms awkwardly –like she’s fighting a battle against her own limbs.
“What’s going on with you, Xenia?” My stomach clenches. “You’ve been twitchy since we got here.”
“Sorry.” Xenia squeezes her eyes shut. “I think I’m still uploading memories or something.”
“Anyway.” She raises herself to her knees, meeting my eyes. “I’m going with Luke and a couple of the others from the Security and Wildlife Committee to check out the drop spot.”
“We want to leave as soon as possible.” Xenia grins as she opens her arms up. “So can I get a hug?”
The blood drains from my face. “Don’t go without me,” I blurt. “I want to go with you!”
“What?” Xenia laughs. “It’s been quite a while since you exercised your melee skills.”

I sit up, raising myself to Xenia’s eye level. “I held my own against Darcy when I barely had any combat experience.” My indignation suddenly overrides my self pity. “I can kick a Dino Nuggets ass just as hard as you can!”
“You’re probably right, Jenna.” Xenia reaches out, gripping my shoulder. “But we already decided on the team for Operation Rapunzel Robinhood.”

Slumping forward, I collapse against my friend, letting the exhaustion, sorrow, and overwhelming realness of the last few days flow out of me in a snotty, babbling fit as I cling to my oldest friend. As she rests her chin on my bare shoulder, I feel Xenia’s left eye give another spastic twitch against my collarbone. Letting out a worried sigh, I pull Xenia tighter. Her eyes relax.

By the time I push back, wiping my nose with the back of my greasy hand, the camp is abuzz with chaotic motion. Finn and Luke are a few yards away, kneeling over a mess of slender juvenile dino ribs and a ragged sheet of parched, yellowish belly-hide. They’re grumbling as they struggle to loop coarse hair-twine around the bones.
"It's too heavy anyway," Luke grunts, tossing a broken chunk of rib aside. "Even if we make it look like a kite, the wind’ll just slam it into the cliff face."
“What’re you fish brains doing?” Xenia gawks at the pile of bones at Luke’s feet.
“We’re going to use the kite to communicate with you.” Finn claps his hands. “I learned Morse code from listening to boats.” His chest swells with pride.

My overwhelming need to be helpful suddenly overrides my self-pity. "Move." I step between the frustrated boys, taking a seat on the cold hard granite. My fingers struggle to grip the greasy twine, but as soon as I touch the raw, leathery hide, three lifetimes of muscle-memory take over. Generations of popsicle-stick kites, torn jackets and trussed Thanksgiving turkeys have prepared me for this moment.

"I think you were pulling the frame too tight on the cross-beam," I mutter, ignoring Finn as he leans over my shoulder, idly popping spit bubbles in my ear. Taking a strand of the fine hair threads—the stuff we spun from the softer, inner layers of our locks—I use a sharp splinter of lightning glass to punch clean, uniform holes through the dino membrane. "If the hide isn't balanced across the keel, the vacuum from the draft will tear it to pieces before it clears the ledge."

For twenty minutes, I don't think about Myka, or the death march my friends are about to take. I just picture the finished product and sew. Wrapping the coarse twine in tight, interlocking hitch knots around the hollow, bird-like bones, I bind the greasy leather until it’s taut as a drum.

When I lift it, the grotesque dino-skin-diamond catches the frigid updraft, tugging against my palm like an eager puppy. It's hideous—flecked with dried feathers and blood—but it's perfectly balanced.
"What a beautiful kite, Jenna," Finn coos, a massive grin breaking through the dirt on his face. "It’s going to swim through the sky just like a fish!"
"Yeah, I think it should do the trick!" I hand the tether over to him.

“Beautiful work Jenna.” Diego admires the kite putting his hand up for a high five. We slap hands and he turns to Xenia. “Get your team together. You want to get to that drop zone before the animals come out of hiding.”

The rope is still anchored to the stalagmite from when The Gleam abandoned us, its length trailing down the dark groove into the abyss. Hitching his dino-leather sack of rations over his shoulder, Luke nods at Xenia. “You ready?”

Before turning to the edge, he kneels by the scorched crater where the smaller Dino Nugget died, hammering a heavy chunk of granite against the floor. With a sharp crack, he breaks free a palm-sized wedge of rock fulgurite.
“If we find a clearing—” Luke slips the sharp, reflective glass shard into the bundle of meat on his back “—we can flash Morse back up to the mountain.

I walk with them to the precipice of Hopeful Mountaintop. Standing at the edge, the sheer scale of New Earth hits my chest—a suffocatingly dense expanse of swaying green branches stretching as far as I can see in any direction.
Xenia steps up to the line first. She looks back at me, her gaze steady. "Don’t let us get lost out there."

Before I can reply, she snatches up the hair-twine rope, plants her feet against the sheer granite face, and leans back into the empty air. I watch her descend, step by treacherous step, until the shadows of the massive trees swallow her whole.

Behind me, Finn lets out a sharp whistle, releasing the frame. The grotesque skin-kite catches the mountain wind, soaring up into the pastel sky—a lonely, leathery beacon dancing above the rock, waiting for the away team to look up.

paragraphs.text: PREVIEW OF HYPERSPEAR YEAR ZERO CHAPTER-7
7 - The Arena
New Earth - The Arena
Xenia’s POV -

The coarse hair-twine rope bites into my raw palms as I brace my bleeding feet against the sheer cliff face. Below me, the canopy is a swaying ocean of vibrant leaves. “Looks clear down there!” I call up, the wind snatching the words from my mouth as Luke, ten yards above me, sits dangling his bare legs over the precipice of the cliff, waiting to start his descent.
I’m basking in the raw thrill—the terrifying beauty of actual gravity—when my left eye violently twitches.

Suddenly a red, wireframe grid snaps into place over the verdant foliage on the left side of my vision. A red arrow pulses aggressively in my peripheral, locking onto a bulky, hairy figure stalking through the underbrush. Red text appears below the beast: “423M away, extremely large reptile.” The sudden overlay obliterates my depth perception and I fumble the rope, plunging for one horrific microsecond, towards the green abyss.
A surge of electric current hijacks my motor cortex and my left hand mechanically clamps onto the rope. The slack goes taut. My shoulder makes a sickening “POP” and I scream in agony.

“Oof” I slam hard against the rock face, tears burning in my eyes as I brace for a fatal fall. But some superhuman force keeps my bleeding, rope-burned hand clasped like a vise —even though the ball of my left shoulder has been wrenched from the socket.
Dry-heaving from the blinding pain, I will my fingers to let go —let me have the sweet relief at the end of the fall.
My grip tightens.
“You okay?” Luke’s quavering voice floats down from thirty feet above.
“Yup-yup!” I wince. “All good.”
Sobbing, I clasp my right hand around the rope. Running my toes along the cliff face, I find a narrow ledge that will bear my weight and ease myself onto it.
The electric grip in my forearm releases. My shoulder explodes with pain as my left hand falls completely limp against my hip.
Breathing heavily, I lean my chest against the cold stone cliff, wedging my limp left wrist into a crack in the rock. Bracing my feet, I throw my body weight forward and down.
White-hot stars explode in my vision, as the joint snaps back into place with a nauseating clunk.
“See? I told you I’m more helpful than that Glitch, Jenna,” Fayezilla’s voice buzzes against my left eardrum like an audio file playing through a broken headset.
“You could’ve killed us, you crazy stowaway.” I mutter under my breath, squinting my left eye shut until the neon red targets disappear.

“Oh please, you would’ve died yesterday in that Dino Nugget fight if I didn’t highlight that femur bone for you.” Fayezilla chides. “Anyway, stop talking to yourself or they’ll kick your crazy ass out of the tribe.”
Tuning out the chatter of my brain-roommate, I launch myself backward into the foliage of a massive nut tree behind me.
My wounded shoulder screams in pain as branches, thick with fan-shaped leaves, whip my face, snapping under my weight as I crash land in a prone position atop a thick horizontal bough.

A strange buzz, like an industrial fan, kicks on above me. Looking up through the broken branches, I catch sight of a cluster of fist-sized, jade-colored beetles, apparently disturbed by my fall, and now swarming toward my face.

Wrapping my legs around the bough, I pull a glistening, jagged shard of Fulgurite from my dino-skin backpack and use it to hurriedly saw off a fan-leafed switch. Swinging the branch like a racket through the crazed flurry, I send a cascade of battered exoskeletons and wings crashing down through the trees.
“What’s going on?” Luke calls down from the top of the cliff behind me.
“I made it to the canopy.” I call up to him as I swat a cluster of glistening beetles against the tree trunk. “There’s a huge ginkgo-looking tree right by the cliff.”
“I’m coming down.” Luke shouts.
I cinch up my tube dress, and take a moment to pick tree debris out of my shaggy bob before getting back to battering the emerald-fist beetles.
I’ve thinned the swarm to less than ten when Luke calls out. “I’m jumping for the tree now.”
A moment later, his muscular form is crashing down through the branches above.
Thudding to a stop, he wrestles himself to an awkward perch on a neighboring bough.
“Oh no!” Luke yelps as the remaining beetles make a beeline towards him.
Bending down a springy bough behind him, Luke scrambles backward, continuing to hold the branch down as he steps over it.
Just before the beetles reach him, Luke releases the bough, batting the bugs in all directions.
“Nice!” I congratulate my number two as I mentally urge Fayezilla to run a sweep below.
“Should we come down or hold tight?” Alana’s voice echoes down from above the trees.
Fayezilla’s scan highlights the location of a possible swamp a short distance from the base of the tree.
“Let Luke and I go down first, Alana.” I bark. “We’ll find a clearing and use our Fulgurite to signal up the mountain.”
My shoulder continues to throb as Luke and I lower ourselves down through the branches of the fan-leafed tree.
I pause when we’re ten feet off the ground. The forest is eerily quiet.
With quiet synchronicity, we lower ourselves to hang from the bough. I keep my agonizing left arm pinned to my side, my right arm hooked around the branch I drop down to the ground.
“I think I saw a swamp through the trees.” I whisper.
Luke goes still. “I think I hear splashing over there.” he cocks his head. “I think the big swamp we saw from the mountaintop is this way.” He points to the right.
The forest floor is densely shaded and eerily calm as we sidle between tall ferns and horsetails towards the increasingly loud buzz of bug wings and the gentle slosh of water against tree roots.

We step out of the shadowy forest onto the sunlit bank of a slow moving river delta and Luke, slipping his dino-skin pack from his back, retrieves a polished piece of lightning glass. “There’s a little hill over by the water.” He trots off towards a pile of straw and debris at the water’s edge. “Should be a good place to try to refract a signal up to my dad and the others.”
Luke scrambles up the mound and I hear a wet crunch under his foot, like a giant egg cracking.
Fayezilla’s voice reverberates in my head. “There’s something big in the water over there.”
My left eye blinks tumultuously as she and I struggle to gain control of my occipital lobe.
”We don’t get to respawn if we die” Fayeyzilla protests, “Let me use our eye!”
I relax my control and the left side of my view highlights an approaching figure. Before I can read the display, a surge of energy seizes my vocal chords.
“Giant—crocodile—Run!” The garbled warning blasts out of my mouth.
For a brief moment my body goes rigid, paralyzed with fear as I catch sight of an eight ton crocodile, gliding through the murky water towards Luke.
A surge of pure adrenaline numbs the pain in my shoulder and I dart away from the water as hard and fast as my new Earth legs will carry me.
Glancing back, I see Luke pulling away from the SUV-sized creature. He’s coming up fast on my right flank.
I hurtle over a thick fern and Luke runs along beside me.

The sound of the crocodile is fading. I peer over my shoulder and catch sight of the massive creature throwing its head back before letting out a deafening, pulsating shriek so powerful the water on its back vibrates off, forming a wet cloud around its body.
“I think she’s going back to her nest.” Luke pants, slowing his pace.

“That might be a good spot over there,” my chest heaves as I point to a spot ahead where the giant redwoods give way to low ferns. Sunlight pours through the massive gap in the canopy illuminating a small swamp —a little bigger than an Olympic pool.

Ripping a hefty piece of redwood bark from a nearby tree, I amble over to the edge of the murky water. I toss the bark into the center of the muddy pool and it lands with a splash. A few salamander-looking amphibia scuttle to the edges of the swamp, but there doesn’t seem to be any angry crocodiles in its depths.
“This looks like a perfect spot to have the rest of the team meet us.” I grip my left shoulder tenderly, flashing a pained smile at Luke.

Luke, angles the glassy, lightning-fused core of his Fulgurite toward the sun, adjusting the refracted beam of white light until it’s a shining dot on the dino skin kite that’s flying above the edge of Hopeful Mountaintop.
A distant cheer echoes down from the mountaintop.
“I’ll Morse code to the team that they should come down and meet us here,” Luke gushes.
Sub-header Title
**** Three Hours Later ****
When Alana, Dexter, and Cade arrive at our swamp, Alana pulls a rolled shred of dino skin from her makeshift backpack.
“The cartography committee mapped a course from this location to the drop zone.” She grins points to some smudges of fat on the skin. “We should pass a couple more swamps about this size on the way.”
Alana rolls up the map. “We can check back in with the Hopeful Mountaintop team when we hit those spots.”
“Great work,” I nod approvingly, but my left eye twitches. I know the map is flawed.

Before we left, Fayezilla had somehow projected a massive, mathematically perfect spatial grid straight into my mind's eye. It was a complete three-dimensional mesh of the entire mountain basin—altitudes, canopy density, and hidden ravines—stored away in her fairy brain in like an unredacted asset file that only she can access.
”Didn’t that crappy-map lady say she used to be a field doctor in a first person shooter gameworld.” Fayezilla chimes in my brain.
Flashing a smile, I take the rolled map. “By the way—” I gaze imploringly at Alana “—You’re a Dr, right? Can you look at my left shoulder?”
Using her dino-skin backpack and some hair twine from my tube dress, Alana quickly binds my wounded arm against my chest in a make-shift sling.
“Thanks friend!” I let out a sigh, finally feeling a faint bit of relief.
Pumping my right fist in the air, I step back to face all four of my comrades and holler: “Let’s go get our loot!”
Our small troop gives a hearty cheer and we set off through the dark, quiet forest.

As the sun rises in the sky, the humid air becomes increasingly thick with the stench of mold, decaying plants, and our own BO. It’s a slow miserable trek, sloshing across shallow swamps, scrambling over mossy, fallen trees and plowing through scratchy underbrush, but except for a few catatonic lizard-like creatures paralyzed by the morning’s acoustic shock, the five of us are the only animals in sight.

After about two miserable hours, we’re all dehydrated, covered in tiny scratches and utterly spent and we’re only halfway to the ionization zone. I’ve given my left eye over to Fayezilla who has been fruitlessly scanning for water.
I’m starting to panic when the dank forest opens into a clearing.

The black loam beneath our feet is completely demolished. Massive, three-toed tracks the size of dinner plates are slowly filling with slow-seeping water. A whole herd, with expansive stride lengths, tore through here.
”I think there’s water nearby.” Fayezilla enthuses in my mind.
“Halt.” I croak, holding my right fist up at a ninety-degree angle.
The others stop behind me.
Easing myself to my knees, I peer down at the mud. Small mammalian paws and the sharp, delicate slashes of avian claws, all heading in the exact same direction.
I run my dry tongue over my cracked lips. "Animals come here for water." My throat is like sandpaper. "The blast this morning panicked them, but they’ll be back.”
“Then let's go get a drink while we can.” Luke sputters, striding up beside me.

We follow the muddy highway for about fifty yards, until the dense redwoods open into a shaded limestone hollow. There, bubbling cleanly out of a fractured rock shelf, is an artesian spring. Crystal-clear water pools into a gravel-bottomed basin, completely free of the murky swamp muck we'd been wading through.
Gleefully, we sprint towards the trough, like school children let out for recess.
Tipping forward, I sip directly from the basin. It’s the most glorious thing I’ve ever tasted. Crisp and cool and so amazingly wet.
After my thirst finally feels satiated. I turn to the group. “We should set up camp and decide on sleeping shifts.”
“Camp?” Cade, gripes. “But we’re so close!”
“The thing that we’re walking towards is an ionization beam.” I scoff. “It’s like a giant storm cloud on the ground.”
“You’re afraid of clouds?” Cade mocks.

Stepping towards him, I narrow my eyes. "We’re like ninety percent water. If we step into that zone, we won’t just get shocked. Our bodies will become a lightning rod.” My chest heaves. “The charge will surge up through our feet, vaporize our blood, and exit through our skulls before we can blink.”

Cade eyes the others, who are also looking at him like he’s a moron. “Fine. I’m not tired. I can take the last sleeping shift.” He skulks over to the trunk of a young conifer, crossing his arms as he leans back against it.
Luke steps behind me resting his hand on my right shoulder. “We can’t just chill here indefinitely.” He whispers “The animals are going to eventually choose water over blind fear.”

After signaling up the mountain and updating our map we continue our march towards the giant blue-white beam blazing down from the sky. The stampede did a good job of clearing a path to the drop zone, so the hike is much less arduous than the first half.

We’re about a thousand yards from the beam of light, and utterly spent when the hairs on my arms begin to stand on end. The air crackles and the air is acrid with the bleach-like sting of concentrated ozone.
Stopping, I face my team, I clear my parched throat and yell over the continuous, bone-rattling roar of the ionization cloud. “We’re getting too close.”
Shading my eyes I peer around the trampled wasteland that surrounds us. “We should back track a little and look for a camping spot.”
“How ‘bout over by that smoldering Tyrannosaurus?” Alana tips her head towards a grotesquely beautiful scorched carcass the size of a school bus, lying a football-field away.
“I’m beginning to love lightning meat.” Cade gushes as he runs towards the T-rex.
Sub-header Title
**** The next morning***

When the ion beam finally retracts back into the sky at dawn, the sudden silence is deafening. With full bellies and eager hearts, we rush forward, our bare feet eagerly slapping the warm cracked earth. By the time we’re a couple hundred yards away, I can see thick plumes of white steam hissing out of the cracks where the subsurface moisture is still boiling. The caustic ozone fumes over power me and I double over coughing.
My eyes water as I gawk at the fifty-foot clearing around the drop zone. It’s a circle of absolute devastation —a stark, glassy crater of fused black sand and volcanic ash.
The steam is too thick to see exactly what’s in the drop zone, but there seems to be a single metal object, shimmering like a mirage in the center of the smoking wasteland.
“We should—” I cover my face with my right arm, “—go back to the T-rex.” I cough. “It’s going to stay hot for a while.”
We pass an anxious couple hours picking over the Tyrannosaurus, looking for useable scraps of dino-leather and snacking on BBQ’d meat before heading back to the scorched clearing.
When we arrive, there’s a single metal object gleaming in the center of a smoldering twenty foot deep crater: A cook pot, big enough to boil a pig, with an interlocking lid.
“Is that it?” Cade moans. “We came all this way for some freaking cookware?”
A smile dances across my lips. “Hell yeah we did!”
With my good arm, I begin unwinding my hair dress.
“We have fresh water nearby now, and meat and this seems like a fairly defensible location.” I gesture to the pot. “If we only get one thing, this is exactly what we need.”
“Go get our prize!” I thrust the end of my hair rope towards Cade. “We’ll all pull you up.” I grin at the rest of my team.

Grabbing the rope, Cade marches to the edge of the crater. Luke, Alana and I take up the slack, helping him ease down the hot jagged embankment. In three leaping steps, Cade bounds to the center of the crater, stopping in front of the three-foot tall cooking vessel. The instant he touches it, a burst of white-blue light extends down from the sky several miles away. “Brace yourselves for the shockwave.” I scream, covering my ears.
